title: Adam, a Type of the One to Come
english: …mystery of the dispensation in the flesh. How, then, does he call him “the one to come” (Romans 5:14)? someone might perhaps ask. For having set before us the first man and recalled the times of the transgression, he named Christ the one who would be present after those times, and the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45). He had indeed been foreordained as Saviour and Redeemer in the will and forethought of God the Father, but he appeared at his own proper times, those the Sovereign willed (1 Timothy 6:15); and these are the times at the end, at the sunset, as it were, of the present age.

So, having made the second correspond to the type of the first, he all but questions his hearer, speaking the next words with a pause, as a question: “But is it not so with the free gift as with the trespass?” (Romans 5:15). It is as if he were saying: We were condemned to death through the transgression in Adam, since the whole of human nature suffered this in him, for he was the firstfruits of the race; but in Christ we blossomed again into life. And Adam was a type of the one to come (Romans 5:14), that is, of Christ, who brings in for us a grace equal in measure to the perversity of those who went before. Have I, then, he says, missed the truth in saying this? Am I carried beyond what is reasonable? Is it not so with the free gift as with the trespass? Or did death prevail through one, while life through one will be powerless? And yet how is it not true to say this: “For if by the trespass of the one the many died, much more have the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abounded for the many” (Romans 5:15)? For the Creator, since he loves mankind, will by no means allow death to prevail through the one, and the life that comes through one man to accomplish nothing. Grace will rise above what comes from wrath.

“And the gift is not as it was through the one who sinned” (Romans 5:16). He refers, as it were, the nature of the matter and the force of the thought to what most befits God. For if, he says, the condemnation that came from one, that is, through one, Adam, passed on to all after his likeness (for, as I said, he was the root of the race and suffered corruption), how could it not be both acceptable to faith and dear to God that many should be justified from many trespasses by one act of righteousness (Romans 5:16)? Or is saving not what God prefers to destroying? Just as, then, Adam was condemned, and the power of the curse prevailed over Moses, making those on earth subject to corruption, so, since Christ, the second Adam, has been justified, justification will surely travel to us as well along the same road as the first. We say that Christ has been justified, not as though he had once been unrighteous and then advanced to justification by progress toward better things, but because he himself, first and alone of men on earth, “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22).

“For if, by the trespass of the one, death reigned through the one,” and so on (Romans 5:17). See again how he reckons the grace that justifies stronger than the curse that condemns. For no one, he says, could claim it was fitting that death through one should prevail over those on…

title: How the Many Were Made Sinners
english: …earth, while life had no share of strength. For much more will those who have the grace that comes through Christ and the gift of righteousness from the bounty above shake off the power of death and reign together with Christ, who gives life to all things (Romans 5:17).

“Therefore, as through one trespass there came condemnation for all people,” and so on (Romans 5:18). To the thoughts already set out the inspired Paul adds, as it were, the conclusion, saying, “Therefore, as through one trespass,” and what follows. For we were condemned in Adam, as I said before, and death, which came from the curse, passed as from the first root into all that sprang from it. But we have been justified and have sprouted again into life, since Christ was justified on our behalf. For our forefather disregarded the commandment given to him, offended God, and underwent what comes from divine wrath, for he slid into corruption. Then sin also burst into human nature; and so the many were made sinners (Romans 5:19), that is, those throughout the whole earth.

But someone might say: Yes, Adam slipped, and because he disregarded the divine commandment he was condemned to corruption and death. But then how were the many made sinners because of him? What are his failings to us? And how at all were we, who had not yet been born, condemned along with him? And this although God says, “Fathers shall not die for their children” (Deuteronomy 24:16), nor children for their fathers; “the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:20). What, then, would be the way of our defence? Certainly, “the soul that sins, it shall die”; but we became sinners through Adam's disobedience in the following way.

He had been made for incorruption and life, and in the paradise of delight he lived a life fit for the holy. His mind was wholly and constantly taken up with the vision of God, and his body was in calm and stillness, with every shameful pleasure at rest, for there was no tumult of unruly impulses in him. But when he fell under sin and slid into corruption, from then on pleasures and impurities rushed into the nature of the flesh, and the law that rages in our members sprang up (Romans 7:23). So nature caught the sickness of sin through the disobedience of the one, that is, Adam. In this way the many were made sinners (Romans 5:19): not as having transgressed together with Adam, for they did not yet exist at all, but as being of his nature, which fell under the law of sin.

Just as, then, human nature fell sick with corruption in Adam through disobedience, and so the passions slipped into it, so it has been set free again in Christ; for he became obedient to God the Father (Philippians 2:8) and committed no sin (1 Peter 2:22).

“The law came in, so that the trespass might increase” (Romans 5:20). Someone, he says, will reasonably argue along these lines and say: Adam “was a type of the one to come” (Romans 5:14), and just as we were made sinners in him through the transgression, so in Christ we have been justified through obedience. Then, he says, the justification in Christ should have appeared to those on earth with nothing coming in between.

title: Why the Law Came In
english: …What need, then, was there, as a matter of necessity, for the laws given through Moses? Against such thoughts the inspired Paul all but rises up again, saying, “The law came in, so that the trespass might increase” (Romans 5:20). The words “came in” mean that the law was brought in between the condemnation in Adam and the righteousness in Christ. And if one asks again what need there was for the law’s coming in, he will hear Paul say plainly, “So that the trespass might increase.” What are you saying, Paul? Was the law, then, also a promoter of sin, and has the trespass multiplied through it? By no means.

We must, then, open out more fully the way this sacred teaching works. David said, accordingly, “All have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there was none who did good, there was not even one” (Psalm 14:3). For after the transgression in Adam all who were on the earth had corrupted their way (Genesis 6:12). That is why they were punished: all of them together underwent a common penalty, the flood, and they were also punished in particular ways, at certain times and in certain lands and cities. For even though there was no law, human nature was still being trained by God, through its inborn impulses, toward the knowledge of what is good.

So God took pity on those on earth, who were faring wretchedly, and in his love of goodness he planned to set them free in Christ from the sin that tyrannized them. But he judged, and very rightly, that those on earth must first be shown to be gravely sick, so that the justification in Christ might then be seen to make its entry into the world as something most needed. For we say that it is not the one already righteous who is justified, but whoever is liable for sins. How, then, were those on earth to be shown beforehand as needing the grace that is in Christ? “The law came in, so that the trespass might increase” (Romans 5:20); that is, so that among those under the law the trespass might appear great, since plainly no one could be justified because of the weakness of nature, and all, as it were, fell under the charges that arise from transgression. The law, then, was laid down as a kind of proof of the weakness of all, so that human affairs might be seen to need the healing that comes through Christ alone. That is why he says, “But where sin increased, grace overflowed all the more” (Romans 5:20). For grace had to be so great that it would be seen to surpass the law that condemns.

“Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus…?” (Romans 6:3). As all agree, we have been baptized into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). Yet if he should say that we have been baptized into Christ Jesus, he will not be speaking beyond what is reasonable. It is quite true that by names, by hypostases, and by the differences of the persons, the Father stands apart from the Son in a certain particular otherness, and the Spirit from both. For the Father is the Father and not the Son; again, the one who is from him by nature is the Son and not the Father; and the Holy Spirit is, in his own proper way, the Spirit. But since the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son (John 14:10), and the Holy Spirit is in both because the substance is the same, then even if someone names only one, by the force of the ideas involved, the declaration of the whole…
translator_notes: Opens mid-argument: εἶτα ποία ... ἡ χρεία finishes the objector's question begun at the end of u02-rem-mid (if justification in Christ was to appear with nothing in between, why the Mosaic law?). The leading ellipsis marks the join.
Ends mid-sentence: the main verb ἐποιήσατο stands at the start of u03-open; the closing ellipsis marks the break. Nothing supplied.

τὸ δέ Παρεισῆλθεν, ἀντὶ τοῦ παρεισβέβληκε: Cyril glosses the verb; rendered as 'the law was brought in between', keeping his point that it stands between Adam's condemnation and Christ's righteousness.
πρόξενος: 'one who brings about, procures'; rendered 'promoter of sin'.
ἰδικῶς δὲ καὶ κατὰ καιροὺς καὶ κατὰ χώρας τε καὶ πόλεις: the verb ἐκολάζοντο is carried over from the previous clause ('they were also punished in particular ways').
The Trinitarian sentence keeps Cyril's terms: ὑποστάσεσι = hypostases, προσώπων = persons, οὐσίας = substance. ἰδικὴν ἑτερότητα = 'particular otherness'.
Subject of λέγοι ('if he should say') is Paul, left as 'he' as in the Greek.
